lesson.title: A Mitochondrial Relay Race Toward Oxygen
lesson.summary: The mitochondrial electron transport chain is a series of protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane that passes electrons from NADH and FADH2 down an energy gradient to oxygen, using the released energy to pump protons across the membrane.
lesson.body:
Everything the Krebs cycle harvested as NADH and FADH2 finally gets put to use in the electron transport chain, a series of four major protein complexes embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane. The chain's job is to pass electrons from one complex to the next, each transfer releasing a bit of energy, until the electrons reach their final destination: molecular oxygen, which combines with the electrons and protons to form water. This is the reason organisms that use aerobic respiration require oxygen at all; without it there, electrons would have nowhere left to go and the whole chain would back up and stall.

Complex I, NADH dehydrogenase, accepts electrons from NADH, oxidizing it back to NAD+ so it can be reused by glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, and the Krebs cycle. Complex II is succinate dehydrogenase, the same enzyme from the Krebs cycle mentioned earlier, and it feeds electrons from FADH2 into the chain at a slightly lower energy level than Complex I does. That difference matters: because FADH2's electrons enter later and at lower energy, they contribute to less proton pumping overall than NADH's electrons do, a fact that becomes important when tallying total ATP yield. From both entry points, electrons pass to a mobile lipid-soluble carrier called ubiquinone, or coenzyme Q, then to Complex III, cytochrome bc1, then to another mobile carrier called cytochrome c, and finally to Complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase, which passes the electrons to oxygen.

The real payoff of this relay is not the electron transfer itself but what it powers along the way. Complexes I, III, and IV use the energy released as electrons move to lower-energy states to actively pump protons, H+ ions, from the mitochondrial matrix across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space. Complex II does not pump protons, which is another reason FADH2-derived electrons ultimately support less ATP synthesis than NADH-derived electrons. This pumping is only possible because the enzymes are held in a fixed orientation by a membrane, connecting back to the cofactor and coenzyme chemistry, NAD+, FAD, and the iron-containing heme groups of the cytochromes, that make each complex capable of accepting and releasing electrons at precisely tuned redox potentials.

The net effect across the whole chain is a steep, one-directional gradient of protons stacking up outside the inner membrane, in the intermembrane space, while the matrix becomes comparatively depleted of protons and more negatively charged. That gradient is not a byproduct to be discarded, it is the entire point of running the electron transport chain in the first place: it stores usable energy in the form of a proton gradient across a membrane, ready to be spent. What happens with that stored energy, how it actually gets converted into ATP, is the subject of oxidative phosphorylation and chemiosmosis, the two ideas that complete the story the electron transport chain sets up here.
